title: Review: Orbits; Center of mass by integration; Inertial vs gravitational mass and the equivalence principle
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Physics C: Mechanics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: C05-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; C05-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; NEW-mass-equivalence-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; NEW-mass-equivalence-1#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: C05-1#N.6, NEW-com-calc-1#N.8, NEW-mass-equivalence-1#N.6, NEW-com-calc-1#N.6, NEW-mass-equivalence-1#N.8, NEW-com-calc-1#N.2, NEW-mass-equivalence-1#N.2, NEW-mass-equivalence-1#N.4, NEW-mass-equivalence-1#N.9. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Centripetal force
items.clue: Role played by gravity for a satellite moving in a circle.

items.label: Period
items.clue: T for one trip around a planet; its square is proportional to r³.

items.label: Equivalence principle
items.clue: In an accelerating frame, apparent weight cannot be told apart from a force of gravity.

items.label: Gravitational mass
items.clue: How strongly an object attracts, and is attracted by, other bodies; appears in Gm₁m₂/r².

questions.stem: Tethys and Rhea are moons of Saturn, and their orbits may be taken as circular. Tethys has an orbital radius of 2.95 × 10⁸ m and a period of 1.89 days. Rhea has an orbital radius of 5.27 × 10⁸ m. What is the period of Rhea?
A thin, uniform wire of linear mass density λ is bent into a semicircle of radius R, centered on the origin and lying in the region y ≥ 0 of the xy-plane. Where is the wire's center of mass?

Ball 1 has mass m and ball 2 has mass 3m. They are released from rest at the same height near Earth's surface, and air resistance is negligible. F₁ and F₂ are the magnitudes of the gravitational forces exerted on the balls by Earth, and a₁ and a₂ are the magnitudes of their accelerations. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: F₂ = F₁ and so a₂ = a₁

questions.stem: A solid sphere of radius R has a volume mass density that decreases from its center to its surface as ρ(r) = ρ₀(1 − r²/R²), where r is the distance from the center and ρ₀ is a positive constant. What is the total mass of the sphere?

A student wakes in a closed, windowless room. A ball she releases accelerates toward the floor at 4 m s⁻², measured relative to the room, and a scale under her reads 40% of her weight on Earth. Which situation could explain both readings?

options.text: Only a room at rest on a planet where g = 4 m s⁻²
Only a rocket in deep space accelerating at 4 m s⁻²
A planet where g = 4 m s⁻², or a rocket accelerating at 4 m s⁻²
A room falling freely toward a planet, with no other forces on it

questions.explanation: Both give a floor force of m × 4 m s⁻² (40% of m × 10 m s⁻²) and a ball that reaches the floor at 4 m s⁻² relative to the room. By the equivalence principle, she cannot tell which.

questions.stem: A thin, nonuniform rod of length L and total mass M lies along an axis from ℓ = 0 to ℓ = L. The mass of the part of the rod between ℓ = 0 and any position ℓ is m(ℓ) = Mℓ³/L³. What is the linear mass density of the rod at position ℓ?

On the International Space Station, an astronaut has two closed toolboxes that look identical; one is full of tools and the other is empty. Both float freely. Which method would let her tell which toolbox is full?

options.text: Rest each one on her palm and feel which one presses down harder.
None will work: with no weight, every object is as easy to start and stop.
Push each with the same small force; see which speeds up less.
Release both at the same height and see which one drifts down faster.

questions.stem: On Earth, a rock on one pan of an equal-arm balance is balanced by 4.0 kg of standard masses on the other pan. The balance, the rock and the standard masses are taken to the Moon, where the gravitational field strength is 1.6 N kg⁻¹. Use g = 10 m s⁻² on Earth. What mass of standard masses balances the rock on the Moon?

options.text: Only 0.64 kg of standard masses is needed to balance it.
A much larger total, 25 kg of standard masses, is now needed.
A total of 6.4 kg of standard masses balances the rock.
The same 4.0 kg of standard masses still balances the rock.

questions.stem: Suppose that for lead only, gravitational mass were 1% larger than inertial mass, while for wood the two were equal. A lead ball and a wooden ball are released together in a vacuum near Earth's surface. How would they fall?

options.text: The lead ball would accelerate at 1.01g and the wooden ball at g.
Both would accelerate at g, since all objects fall together in a vacuum.
The lead ball would accelerate at 0.99g, held back by its extra inertia.
The lead ball would fall faster by an amount set by its weight, so a heavier lead ball would fall faster still.

questions.explanation: With only gravity acting, a = (m_grav/m_inertial)g. For lead the ratio is 1.01, so 1.01g; for wood, g. Experiments find no such difference, to about 1 part in 10¹⁵.
